Title: Project Gutenberg’s licensing paradox: public-domain texts free to use — with trademark and redistribution constraints
Description: Although many Project Gutenberg eBooks are public-domain works that anyone in the U.S. can copy or reuse, the Project Gutenberg License and trademark rules impose specific obligations (keep the license, display a required sentence, and restrict use of the Project Gutenberg brand), creating a practical tension between unrestricted public-domain reuse and legal/brand constraints on redistribution.
Audience: Librarians, educators, small publishers, digital archivists, and anyone who redistributes public-domain texts
Rationale: Readers who plan to copy, redistribute, or republish Project Gutenberg texts often assume public-domain means no conditions. The source shows that while the underlying works may be public domain, Project Gutenberg requires retention of its license text and controls use of its trademark — important legal and practical constraints that affect how these works may be shared or branded.
Evidence: Explicit license and trademark language in the source: “This eBook is for the use of anyone anywhere in the United States… You may copy it, give it away or re-use it under the terms of the Project Gutenberg License” (opening). The license states “Project Gutenberg is a registered trademark” (1.B) and requires a prominent sentence with active links to the full license whenever a Project Gutenberg work is distributed (1.E.1). It also says nearly all individual works are public domain but that removing references to Project Gutenberg is permitted only under specific conditions (1.C).
